summary:
A visitor to Missouri stands under the national framework of the United States in every setting. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F, so a trans visitor's documents may not match their presentation. Airport screening and visa decisions follow the same national rules, including the State Department's February 2025 announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', with a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth capable of being treated as fraud and a permanent bar.

Missouri prohibits gender-affirming medical care for minors. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a St Louis judge denied a preliminary injunction against it on 29 August 2023. The statute bars hormones and puberty blockers for under-18s unless the patient was already in treatment, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.

The SAFE Act also bars MO HealthNet Medicaid coverage of the prohibited care, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes violating providers to licence revocation. CNN reports that the law additionally bars Missouri Medicaid from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, and that doctors who breach the ban can lose their state medical licence and be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment.

Litigation over the ban has failed at every stage so far. Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner filed suit on 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court on behalf of three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA, seeking to block Senate Bill 49 before its 28 August 2023 effective date. A Missouri judge upheld the law on 25 November 2024, and on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld the ban on gender-transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other gender-affirming care for minors, quoting the 2025 United States Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's similar ban. Counsel for the plaintiffs said they would appeal. The ban has been in force since 28 August 2023 and remains in force.

The statute carries a 2027 sunset enacted as a Republican-Democrat concession, but lawmakers have moved to make it permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative also seeks to ban such care indefinitely. The plaintiffs continue toward trial on the merits.

Correctional custody carries its own care exclusion. Governor Mike Kehoe signed an appropriations law, effective 2 July 2026, barring state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri thereby became the seventh state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban gender-affirming care for inmates; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while similar Idaho and Georgia measures were blocked by federal courts.

A trans visitor to Missouri is unlikely to encounter the SAFE Act unless accompanying a minor who needs medical care, but anyone detained in a Missouri jail, prison or correctional centre loses access to state-funded hormone therapy and transition surgery under both the SAFE Act and the 2026 appropriations law.
tangentialFactors:
Missouri's care ban sits inside a wider national pattern rather than standing alone. As of the 2026 appropriations law, six other states had barred gender-affirming care for incarcerated transgender people, and federal courts in Idaho and Georgia blocked comparable measures, so custody outcomes for a trans detainee depend on which jurisdiction is holding them.

The direction of Missouri law is toward expansion rather than retreat. The SAFE Act's 2027 sunset was a negotiated concession, and both a legislative push for permanence and a November 2026 ballot initiative would remove the expiry, while the January 2026 state supreme court ruling relied on the United States Supreme Court's 2025 decision upholding Tennessee's ban.

The federal layer described above remains contested in court: several of the national executive and agency measures have been blocked or enjoined, and the ACLU's suit over passport sex markers is pending, so document and screening outcomes can shift during a stay in Missouri.
localsOnly:
Missouri residents who are minors are barred from starting hormones or puberty blockers under the SAFE Act unless already in treatment on 28 August 2023, and no resident of any age can receive transition surgery as a minor. MO HealthNet, the state Medicaid programme, will not pay for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age.

Providers face real professional exposure: a Missouri medical licence can be revoked for violating the ban, and a patient may sue a doctor up to 15 years after treatment was given.

Residents held in Missouri prisons, jails and correctional centres have no state-funded access to cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery from 2 July 2026, and those already receiving care are not transitioned off it by any taper plan in the appropriations law.

Missouri voters will see a ballot initiative in November 2026 proposing to ban gender-affirming care for minors indefinitely, and the legislature has signalled intent to replace the 2027 sunset with a permanent statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the plaintiffs' promised appeal after the 25 November 2024 ruling proceeded beyond the Missouri Supreme Court's 13 January 2026 decision is unresolved in the available sources; the inventory states only that counsel said they would appeal and that the case was to continue toward trial on the merits.

The interaction between the state care ban and federal custody in Missouri is not sourced. Rules for transgender people held by Federal Bureau of Prisons or Immigration and Customs Enforcement facilities inside the state are governed by national policy and are not addressed by the Missouri statutes described here; no source in this inventory states which regime applies at a given facility.

Whether the SAFE Act's 2027 sunset will actually be repealed, and the outcome of the November 2026 ballot initiative, are unresolved. The inventory records the efforts, not their result.

No source in this inventory addresses Missouri-specific rules on identity documents, birth certificates, driver's licences, bathroom or facilities access, or hate-crime protection for transgender people; those questions must be verified against separate Missouri material.
